# Medicaid Expansion and Mortality Among Formerly Incarcerated Individuals

**Authors:** Benjamin A. Barsky; Mark J. Soto; Benjamin A. Howell; Meredith B. Rosenthal

**Affiliations:** 1University of California College of the Law, San Francisco | 2Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts | 3Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut

## Abstract

This cross-sectional study reports on the association of mortality in formerly incarcerated individuals after the Affordable Care Act allowed states to expand Medicaid coverage.

## Abstract

Is Medicaid expansion associated with lower all-cause mortality among formerly incarcerated individuals, including those in racial and ethnic minority groups?

In this cross-sectional study using difference-in-differences analysis of data on 2 210 000 formerly incarcerated people in 17 states, Medicaid expansion was associated with a 14% lower monthly odds of death. In stratified analyses, Medicaid expansion was associated with a 21% lower monthly odds of mortality among Black individuals and a 15% lower monthly odds of mortality among White individuals; no statistically significant difference was detected among Hispanic individuals.

Results of this study suggest that expanding access to health insurance through Medicaid expansion may reduce mortality among formerly incarcerated people, particularly Black and White people, a population that experiences elevated mortality risks on return into the community.

## Abstract

Most incarcerated individuals eventually return to their communities, where they face high mortality risks that vary by race and ethnicity. The Affordable Care Act allowed states to expand Medicaid to cover all adults aged 18 to 64 years earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level, and expansion has improved health outcomes among the adult population, including mortality; yet research on the formerly incarcerated population remains underdeveloped.

To assess the association between Medicaid expansion and all-cause mortality among formerly incarcerated individuals, including in analyses stratified by race and ethnicity.

Cross-sectional study using stacked difference-in-differences (DID) analysis of individual-level prison release data of formerly incarcerated people in 17 states from January 2010 through December 2020 from the Criminal Justice Administrative Records System linked to the Numerical Identification (Numident) file to create a person-month–level dataset. Dates of data analysis were from August 2024 to December 2025.

Formerly incarcerated individuals released in a Medicaid expansion state.

All-cause mortality, determined by month of death in Numident. The study used a discrete-time proportional hazards model fit with logistic regression to implement the DID approach. Odds ratios (ORs) quantifying differences in monthly postrelease mortality risk are reported. The study population was stratified based on race and ethnicity.

The study population included 2 210 000 formerly incarcerated people in 17 states: American Indian and Alaska Native (14 500 [0.7%]), Asian (16 500 [0.7%]), Black (655 000 [29.6%]), Hispanic (307 000 [13.9%]), and White (1 220 000 [55.1%]); most were men (79.9%), and the plurality were aged 18 to 34 years (45.0%). Expansion was associated with a 14% lower monthly odds of death in the study population (OR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.74-0.99; P = .04). In stratified analyses, expansion was associated with a 21% lower odds of monthly mortality among Black individuals (OR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.68-0.91; P = .002) and a 15% lower odds of monthly mortality among White individuals (OR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.73-0.99; P = .03); expansion was not associated with mortality among Hispanic individuals (OR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.71-1.44; P = .95).

This study found that Medicaid expansion was associated with reduced monthly all-cause mortality after prison release, particularly among Black and White individuals. These findings underscore the importance of extending Medicaid coverage to the reentry population.

## Introduction

The US has more than 20% of the world’s incarcerated population despite comprising only 5% of the global population.1 Most people in prison eventually return to their communities, where they face sharply elevated mortality risks.2 One nationally representative cohort study found that people with incarceration histories have a 39% higher all-cause mortality than people without such histories.3 This finding is consistent with single-state studies and research from outside the US.4,5 Risk of death following release also changes over time, with the highest risk in the immediate postrelease period.5

Racial and ethnic groups experience incarceration unequally. Black and Hispanic individuals are at higher risk of incarceration over their lifetimes compared with White individuals.6 Mortality risk also varies by race and ethnicity, partly due to different underlying patterns of health risks.7,8,9 White individuals have a higher risk of death following release from prison compared with Black and Hispanic individuals.10,11 Differences in cause-specific postrelease mortality also exist between different groups. For example, White and Hispanic individuals are more likely to die due to overdose or suicide and Black individuals are more likely to die due to homicide.12,13,14 Finally, these groups experience differences during the community reentry process in resource access, employment and education opportunities, and importantly, access to high-quality health care, which may explain differences in mortality postrelease.15,16,17

The Affordable Care Act (ACA), passed into law in 2010, enabled states to expand Medicaid coverage to all adults aged 18 to 64 years earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level (FPL) beginning in January 2014. As a result, under Medicaid expansion, an estimated 80% to 90% of previously ineligible people leaving prison were newly eligible for health insurance coverage.18 Notably, previously incarcerated people benefit disproportionately from Medicaid expansion because most do not receive employer-based insurance, are younger than 65 years and not eligible for Medicare, and live in poverty.19 People with criminal involvement experienced a 25% increase in Medicaid enrollment following ACA implementation.19

Medicaid expansions have improved health outcomes among the adult population, including mortality.20,21 Yet research on the formerly incarcerated population remains underdeveloped, not least because of the scarcity of data linking incarceration records with health data. One study conducted by Perera and colleagues,22 limited to 2 states (ie, North Carolina and Rhode Island), found associations between Medicaid expansion and decreased all-cause, overdose, and homicide mortality. Other studies found higher insurance rates, better treatment outcomes, and lower reincarceration rates in expansion states.23 But evidence on health outcomes in this population attributable to Medicaid expansion, including mental health and substance use treatment engagement, is inconclusive.23 A recent single-state study also found no association between Medicaid coverage and criminal charges or convictions.24 Given the Medicaid expansion impact on mortality in the general population and the comparatively high risk of death in the formerly incarcerated population possibly driven by poor access to quality health care, Medicaid expansion plausibly improved mortality outcomes in this population group.

In this difference-in-differences (DID) study, we merged individual-level data from the US Census Bureau to assess the association between Medicaid expansion and all-cause mortality among previously incarcerated individuals. We also stratified results based on race and ethnicity. To our knowledge, this multistate study is by far the largest to study this specific research question.

## Methods

### Data Sources and Study Population

This cross-sectional study used the Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) to identify people with histories of prison incarceration. CJARS is a nationally integrated criminal record repository constructed in collaboration between the US Census Bureau and the University of Michigan.25 It amasses longitudinal electronic records from state criminal justice departments across the country and harmonizes these records to capture episodes throughout all stages of the criminal adjudication process, from arrest through release. Within the protected US Census Bureau computing environment, CJARS data can be used to link individual longitudinal criminal records to other data collected by the US Census Bureau. Because of our focus on the formerly incarcerated population, we only focused on CJARS prison release data. The Institutional Review Board at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health deemed this study exempt from review and the need for informed consent as not human participant research. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.

Leveraging individual-level identifiers (ie, Protected Identification Keys) made available by the US Census Bureau, we linked CJARS data to the Social Security Administration (SSA) Numerical Identification (Numident) file to create a person-month–level dataset. Numident tracks interactions that individuals with Social Security numbers (SSNs) have with the SSA. To link these files, the US Census Bureau assigns Protected Identification Keys to individuals based on all personally identifiable information available in CJARS, which are then linked to SSNs. For this study, the implication is that, as long as someone ever had an interaction with the SSA, linkage between CJARS and Numident would be feasible. Numident records typically include date of birth, place of birth, sex, race and ethnicity, date of SSN application, dates and types of SSA interactions, and date of death, if applicable. The number of months contributed by individuals is based on the fewest months between month of final known release and death, aging into Medicare (65 years), or June 2021 (the most recent data available when beginning our analysis).

We defined our study period from January 2010 through December 2020. Dates of data analysis were from August 2024 to December 2025. Our study population includes people released from prison in 17 states who have prison incarceration records for this period. We removed states whose prison records had known data-reporting problems (eg, Connecticut, New Mexico, Texas). The states ultimately included in our study population incarcerated approximately 41.1% of the total US incarcerated population in 2020.26 Consistent with previously published research, we limited our analysis to the period after the individuals’ last release.27,28

### Treatment, Outcome, and Covariates

We defined our treatment group as individual-level observations in 12 states after they expanded Medicaid during the study period: Arizona, California, Colorado, Illinois, Minnesota, Nevada, and Washington after January 2014; Michigan after April 2014; Pennsylvania after January 2015; Indiana after February 2015; Utah after January 2020; and Nebraska after October 2020. The control group comprised individuals released from 5 states that had not expanded Medicaid during the study period: Florida, Georgia, Kansas, North Carolina, and Wisconsin; among these states, North Carolina expanded Medicaid after the study period. We assumed that people remained in the state in which they served their prison term. Research shows that interstate migrations among formerly incarcerated people are rare; 1 reason relates to restrictions on doing so (eg, parole conditions).29

The study outcome was all-cause mortality, determined using month of death in Numident. Numident computes mortality data based on several sources, including reports of death from family members and representatives, verified reports from friends, state government offices, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Internal Revenue Service.30 Mortality data under the Numident are consistent with published vital statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.30 Using monthly rather than annual mortality data allows for more precise effect estimation relative to expansion timing, especially because of the heightened mortality rate among formerly incarcerated people shortly after release from incarceration.

The covariates included age at release (18-34, 35-49, 50-64 years), sex (male, female), race and ethnicity (American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic, White), incarceration length (<1, 1-2, 2-5, >5 years), and number of previous incarcerations (0, 1, ≥2). We chose these covariates because they are known to be associated with mortality and do not pose any risk of posttreatment bias.

### Statistical Analysis

We calculated standardized mean differences (SMDs) in our covariates between expansion and nonexpansion states for the study period. SMDs represent the difference between the means of 2 groups relative to a common SD; in quasi-experimental studies (ie, research leveraging natural experiments or policy variations to support valid causal inferences), SMDs indicate whether balance exists across covariates in the control and treatment groups. We consider SMD differences less than 0.10 to be negligible. We have rounded all numbers according to the US Census Bureau’s Disclosure Review Board rules.

We used DID methods to estimate the association between Medicaid expansion and mortality among previously incarcerated individuals. This method allows us to compare mortality outcomes before and after expansion among exposed and unexposed person-months. Given the varying dates of Medicaid expansion, we implemented a stacked DID approach.31 We used a discrete-time proportional hazards model fit with logistic regression to perform our DID approach.32 We reported an odds ratio (OR) for the interaction between an indicator for postexpansion and expansion state to quantify the difference in the log-odds of monthly postrelease mortality risk given that the previously incarcerated individuals did not die in an earlier month, adjusting for covariates and state and month-year fixed effects.33

To examine whether mortality trends were similar between treatment and control states before expansion, we generated an event study plot showing adjusted differences in monthly mortality risk pre- and postexpansion. We then stratified our study population based on race and ethnicity and estimated monthly mortality risk within strata; we excluded Asian and American Indian or Alaska Native individuals due to sample size limitations. We used unpaired, 2-tailed t tests with a statistical significance threshold of P < .05; analyses were conducted using Stata, version 18 (StataCorp).

For sensitivity analyses, we first re-estimated our DID coefficient using a continuous-time Cox proportional hazards model. The proportional hazards model assumes a constant proportional treatment effect, which allows the treatment effect to be larger in absolute terms for observable individual characteristics known to be associated with greater mortality risks. We accounted for the varying risk of death over time for individuals postrelease by including the interaction of age and time since release in each month as a time-varying covariate. The interaction allows the hazard ratio to change simultaneously in response to time from release and age at release as opposed to holding the hazard ratio constant for individuals at different ages during the follow-up period. Second, we removed data on people released in Wisconsin because, although it did not expand Medicaid eligibility via the provisions of the ACA, it contemporaneously increased Medicaid eligibility to residents earning less than 100% of the FPL, while residents earning 100% to 133% of the FPL were entitled to ACA exchange subsidies.34 Third, we implemented a placebo test narrowing the study timeline from January 2010 through December 2013 and imposed an artificial treatment date of January 2012 for states eventually expanding Medicaid. Finally, we only included people aging into Medicare (≥65 years) to test our expectation that this population should not experience the benefits of Medicaid expansion.

## Results

The study included 2 210 000 individuals, with 1 180 000 (53.4%) from expansion states and 1 030 000 (46.6%) from nonexpansion states: American Indian and Alaska Native (14 500 [0.7%]), Asian (16 500 [0.7%]), Black (655 000 [29.6%]), Hispanic (307 000 [13.9%]), and White (1 220 000 [55.1%]). We ascertained person-level race and ethnicity data through the US Census Bureau Numident file. Most were men (79.9%) and 20.1% were women, and the plurality were aged 18 to 34 years (45.0%) (Table 1). Of the covariates we adjusted for in our DID models, the following had SMDs greater than 0.10 between expansion and nonexpansion states: Black and Hispanic racial distribution (SMD=0.269 and 0.405), male sex distribution (SMD=0.104), and number of previous incarcerations (SMD=0.204).

During the entire study period, 181 000 individuals in total (8.2%) died after being released from prison (Table 1); 8800 individuals (0.4%) died within 1 month of release, 13 500 (0.6%) within 3 months, and 21 500 (1.0%) within 6 months. In addition, 85 500 (7.3%) occurred in expansion states, and 95 500 (9.3%) occurred in nonexpansion states.

In adjusted logistic models, Medicaid expansion was associated with a 14% lower monthly odds of death (adjusted OR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.74-0.99; P = .04) (Table 2). Adjusted Cox models showed an 18% lower monthly hazard of death (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72-0.94; P = .01) (Table 2).

In sensitivity analyses, results were consistent with our primary mortality analysis when excluding Wisconsin (eTable 1 in Supplement 1). Our placebo treatment (eTable 2 in Supplement 1) and event study (eFigure in Supplement 1) tests provided evidence of no significant differences in monthly mortality between expansion and nonexpansion states. When restricting our sample to people aged 65 years and older, we found that expansion was associated with a 17% lower odds of monthly mortality (OR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.7-0.99; P = .03) (eTable 3 in Supplement 1).

## Discussion

In this DID analysis comprising 2 210 000 formerly incarcerated individuals, Medicaid expansion was associated with a reduction in monthly all-cause mortality among individuals released from prison. People aged 35 years or older had higher ORs than people aged 18 to 34 years, and females had a lower OR than males. On the whole, our findings align with research on the general adult population, which documented a 6% annual relative reduction in mortality post–Medicaid expansion.20

Stratified analyses revealed mortality reductions among Black individuals (21%) and White individuals (15%). These findings contrast with research by Perera and colleagues22 showing no mortality improvements among formerly incarcerated Black people in 1 Medicaid expansion state (ie, Rhode Island). Yet consistent with that research, our findings do not suggest mortality reductions among Hispanic people. Given this, our study builds on the existing literature by finding unequal mortality outcomes among formerly incarcerated racial and ethnic minoritized groups after Medicaid expansion.22

To improve care for formerly incarcerated people and guide policymaking, researchers should examine mechanisms underlying our overall and stratified findings. One hypothesis is that the use of maternal health care postincarceration improved in Medicaid expansion states, thereby reducing peripartum mortality. Limited research, in number of studies and scope, has found an association between Medicaid expansion and higher medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) use among system-involved pregnant women in substance use treatment and better infant health outcomes.35,36 Moreover, research on the general Medicaid population has yielded conflicting conclusions, with evidence showing lower maternal mortality in expansion states, especially among Black women, but no differences in severe maternal morbidity.37,38 On the whole, however, data on incarcerated people who are pregnant or parenting are sparse, supporting the need for increased research attention on the morbidity and mortality impact of health insurance coverage expansions on this population.39

Another hypothesis is that increased access to high-quality mental health care and substance use disorder (SUD) treatment, facilitated by Medicaid coverage, may explain the observed decrease in postrelease mortality in Medicaid expansion states.5 This hypothesis is relevant to the incarcerated population as a whole and to subgroups, including women who are pregnant or parenting. To date, however, research on this issue has been mixed. On the one hand, Perera and colleagues22 found improvements in drug overdose mortality in 1 expansion state and another study found higher use of MOUD.40 Some studies in populations other than this specific population group have also found improvements in SUD, including OUD treatment, after Medicaid expansion.41,42,43 On the other hand, studies have not found a decrease in suicide mortality or unmet mental health care in expansion states among formerly incarcerated individuals.22,44 A potentially effective way to harmonize this heterogeneous research landscape, which uses a range of single-state and multistate data sources, is to link high-quality, individual-level prison release records from many states (eg, through CJARS) with Medicaid administrative claims data (eg, the Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System) to find treatment engagement patterns associated with decreases in postrelease mortality risk.

The prevention of behavioral health–related mortality (eg, overdose deaths) may also explain our stratified results by race and ethnicity. But, here, too, the literature is inconclusive and would benefit from more thorough analyses. Research shows that Medicaid expansion was associated with increased Medicaid coverage for Black, Hispanic, and White people with SUDs.45 At the same time, this same research showed no improvements in SUD treatment among these groups.45 Moreover, studies focusing on people referred to substance treatment facilities through the criminal system found that Black and Hispanic people received OUD treatment less often than White people after Medicaid expansion.40,46 In addition, mental health treatment does not appear to have improved among racial and ethnic minoritized groups after Medicaid expansion.47,48

Other, more indirect, mechanisms may explain Medicaid expansion’s association with improved mortality outcomes among this population. For instance, 1 study focused on Wisconsin found that Medicaid coverage mitigates financial instability for formerly incarcerated people.49 This study suggests that improved mortality outcomes may derive from factors alongside—or beyond—health services engagement postrelease, including Medicaid’s well-documented financial stabilizing benefits.50 In addition, Medicaid expansion may have augmented spending to safety-net facilities (eg, hospitals) and heightened awareness about coverage availability.20 These dynamics may have improved coverage rates and health outcomes, including mortality, among more unexpected groups, including people aged 65 years or older who may not have acquired sufficient Medicare work credits throughout their lives. The latter finding is consistent with research from Sommers and colleagues20 who found all-cause mortality improvements among people aged 65 years and older in Medicaid expansion states.

Our findings underscore the importance of efforts to extend Medicaid coverage to people leaving prison. Medicaid reentry waivers, approved in 19 states and pending in 8 and the District of Columbia, may hold promise because of their focus on facilitating access to MOUDs and continuity of coverage and care during reentry.51 This study suggests the potential protective mortality implications of Medicaid-financed carceral health services targeted toward specific health conditions (eg, mental health disorders, SUD), including for people incarcerated for short time periods. The success of reentry waivers will also depend on community health referrals tailored to the social needs (eg, language-concordant care, geographically accessible services) of formerly incarcerated groups.

### Limitations

Our research has several limitations. First, our sample only includes individuals whose Social Security records are successfully linked to prison records. Second, our sample is limited to states that participated in CJARS data collection. Third, because our data do not include income or Medicaid eligibility information, we cannot identify who is Medicaid-eligible based on income qualifications in any given state. Fourth, by limiting the study population to last prison releases, we may have overlooked the impact of many prison incarcerations on postrelease mortality. Fifth, while we follow best practices for quasi-experimental analysis, we cannot rule out that changes in mortality in expansion states vs nonexpansion states are due to unobserved policies or phenomena. Finally, the Hispanic subgroup analysis may have been underpowered to detect clinically meaningful effects on mortality.

## Conclusions

In this cross-sectional DID study, Medicaid expansion was associated with reduced monthly all-cause mortality among formerly incarcerated people, particularly among Black and White people. These findings underscore the importance of extending Medicaid coverage to the reentry population, including through Medicaid reentry waivers.
